title: HeHalutz in Będzin: From Youthful Resolve to the Road to Palestine
summary: The book gives sustained attention to young Będzin residents who built movements, prepared for pioneering work, and made the dangerous journey to Palestine.

editorialContent:
![Będzin, the town from which young pioneers set out](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/B%C4%99dzin_-_Zamek_obronny_z_XIVw..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)
## A town that was also a crossroads

For Będzin’s young Zionists, the Land of Israel was not just an idea debated in meetings. It was a destination to prepare for—and, at moments of political upheaval, a perilous journey to attempt. The memorial book remembers that passage through youth organisations, practical training, ideological commitment and collective emigration. Its accounts also preserve the uncertainty and improvisation behind the pioneers’ resolve.

Będzin stood in the Zagłębie region, close to shifting borders and industrial towns including Sosnowiec. In its account, the memorial book looks back to a much longer history of movement: it recalls pioneers leaving in the Second Aliyah, including ten young people who went between 1905 and 1907. A separate record describes the first Będzin group’s journey as taking place in 1906. These recollections place the town’s pioneering story before the formal organisation of the later groups, but do not establish one definitive date for the first departure. [The Jewish community of Będzin](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_9efb3bc52c5ccb1275e98a78) formed the setting for those decisions: young people imagining a future beyond the town while their families, work and established lives remained there.

The wider local history helps explain the ferment. Virtual Shtetl places Jewish workers’ parties, including the Bund and Poale Zion, in Będzin during the revolutionary years of 1905–1907, and records a local Zionist Organisation branch in 1922 and the Zionist Labour party Hitachdut in 1925. These were not simply different names for a single movement: they show political and social life expanding through organisations with distinct commitments. The memorial book’s account of HeHalutz, whose name appears inconsistently in the original OCR, describes young people from Tze’irei Zion and Ivriyah organising for practical work. [HeHalutz](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_27798329921e9ffbb46efde6) thus belonged to a wider local landscape of political debate and youth activity, rather than standing alone.

## Training, debate and belonging

The memorial book links the pioneering impulse to organisations that shaped young people before they left. It names [Hashomer](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_e3f4299290d59c83c48236f8), later remembered as Hashomer Hatzair, alongside HeHalutz and Gordonia. These movements offered more than a route to emigration: they created a shared social world of education, collective discipline and arguments about what a renewed Jewish life should look like.

One strand of that world appears in the book’s recollection of Zionist youth singing on Górka. [Zionist youth](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_9d2985ed48c7497be26bc2d0) are remembered not in an office or formal assembly, but together, singing songs associated with Zion. The book names Aryeh Fridler among them. Another supplied record identifies Shpeizer as a Hashomer Hatzair representative delivering greetings, and Arie Lyor thanking those who sent greetings and promising further Gordonian activity. Such fragments suggest lively contact among groups as well as distinctions between them. The records do not provide enough detail to reconstruct every debate or to assign each person to a specific faction beyond what is explicitly stated.

In the broader Polish context, these organisations combined cultural life with preparation for physical work and emigration. Virtual Shtetl’s account of the prewar kibbutz movement describes HeHalutz as a cross-party organisation that became an umbrella for much of Zionist youth activity in Poland during the 1930s; agricultural training centres prepared young people for life in Palestine. That context illuminates what “practical work” could mean in Będzin’s account, but should not be mistaken for proof that every local member followed the same training path. The memorial book’s own testimony is more particular: it recalls people, departures and journeys, rather than offering a complete membership register.

Among the founders it names are [Yaakov Erlich](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_fcacc35e3dd7b2b19754ddbc) and [Yaakov Lasker](/communities/bedzin/records/mention_43bf435d80ffcc359f389951). The book also connects Yakov Gutman with HeHalutz and mentions Gordonia, but the records do not settle the exact role of each named person in founding or leading the organisation. Their presence nonetheless gives the story human scale: an institution remembered through the people who built it and through younger members who took its ideals onto the road.

## Seven set out; six reached Jaffa

The journey that most vividly embodies Będzin’s pioneering resolve began amid the instability at the end of the First World War. The memorial book contains conflicting details that should remain visible. One account says seven young men departed on 31 October 1918; another recalls leaving on 30 October. The supplied event record likewise dates the departure to 30 October. Jakob Lasker recounts that seven set out, but that one mother, Mrs. Birencwajg, caught up with her son in Lwów and brought him home. Six continued.

The book names the young men in overlapping accounts. Yisroel Oppenheim, Yakov Lasker, Kuba Zmigrod, Sender Lubling, Yitzhak Handelsman, Dovid Majteles and Ayshek Birencwajg appear in the recollection of the seven; Lasker’s account identifies Birencwajg as the one who turned back. In Yisroel Oppenheim’s diary, the travelers walk toward the Austrian border, pay smugglers, and continue by rail. Their route passes through Lwów and Odessa, then by ship to Constantinople and onward through Beirut to Jaffa. The diary describes border closures, armed conflict and shortages; Lasker recalls a dangerous passage through an area contested by Polish and Ukrainian forces. These are the pioneers’ own remembered experiences, not a general itinerary for all emigrants.

There is a further discrepancy in how the arrival is framed. A memorial-book heading and supplied event record say that two Będzin groups arrived in Jaffa on 12 December 1918. The detailed testimony about the first group says six reached Jaffa on that date, after a difficult sea passage; Lasker recalls poor conditions aboard ship and illness after arrival. Elsewhere, Shmuel Liwer describes a separate group travelling via Vienna and Trieste. These accounts establish distinct routes and stages of migration, but do not fully reconcile the number of arrivals associated with each group.

The survivors’ later lives are unevenly recorded. The memorial book names Israel Oppenheim, Yakov Lasker, Kuba Zmigrod, Yitzhak Handelsman, Sender Lubling, Dovid Majteles and Ayshek Birncwajg, but its accounts do not give equally clear outcomes for all. It says Lasker and Oppenheim remained in Israel, and that Majteles was killed; another account says Birencwajg later died in Israel. A complete family history cannot be reconstructed from these passages alone.

## The long wait, and a later departure

The route through Italy reveals that commitment did not remove practical barriers. Liwer recalls months waiting in Trieste, with the war and the lack of ships frustrating plans. His account follows the group through Rome and Naples, where the travelers had spent their money and were living on meagre support. The book gives differing measures of the group over time: eight young men from Będzin joined a larger gathering of pioneers, while the wider party later became known as “the 105.” It describes a staged departure through Alexandria and Cairo, with British restrictions allowing only a limited number to travel at once. A separate supplied record characterises the second group’s journey as lasting six months and says that its members were delayed in Italy and elsewhere; the testimonies show a prolonged, complicated passage rather than a single direct voyage.

The story did not end with the 1918–1919 pioneers. The memorial book records another Będzin departure on 4 December 1932, when a selected group left by car for Palestine. That brief entry contrasts sharply with the earlier accounts of foot travel, smuggling, interrupted railways and long waits. It marks a later phase of organised emigration, though the passage supplied here does not identify everyone in the group or explain how candidates were selected.

The contrast between the two periods is significant. In 1918, the road to the Land of Israel ran through collapsing empires and contested borders. By the 1930s, Zionist youth organisations had become part of a broader network of training and migration, while access to Palestine remained constrained. The memorial book preserves the hopeful purpose and the lived obstacles together: songs and organisational life in Będzin, the painful separation from parents, and the exhaustion and uncertainty of travel.

That record is not a complete census of the people who left. It chiefly preserves what survivors remembered and chose to include. Independent local and archival accounts can help situate the movements and the changing political landscape, but they do not fill every biographical gap. What remains clear is that for Będzin’s pioneers, HeHalutz made an ideal tangible: a collective discipline that began in youth, and a journey undertaken despite uncertainty about whether the road would remain open.
